title: Given an array of positive numbers and a target sum, find the length of the smallest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to the target. If no such subarray exists, return zero. (LeetCode: Minimum Size Subarray Sum)
shortTitle: Smallest Subarray with a Given Sum (Variable-Size Sliding Window)

s1_definition.profdef: The smallest-subarray-with-a-given-sum problem uses a variable-size sliding window over positive numbers. You expand the window on the right, accumulating the sum, and whenever the sum reaches the target you shrink from the left as much as possible while staying at or above the target, recording the smallest window length achieved. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh needs to collect at least a target rupee amount from a run of consecutive daily deposits, using the shortest possible stretch of days. He grows his stretch by adding the next day on the right until the total reaches the target, then he trims days off the left as long as the total still meets the target, noting how short the stretch got. He keeps doing this across the whole history and remembers the shortest qualifying stretch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow right until you hit the target, then shrink left as far as you can, tracking the smallest length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The smallest-subarray-with-a-given-sum problem uses a variable-size sliding window over positive numbers. You expand the window on the right, accumulating the sum, and whenever the sum reaches the target you shrink from the left as much as possible while staying at or above the target, recording the smallest window length achieved. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh needs to collect at least a target rupee amount from a run of consecutive daily deposits, using the shortest possible stretch of days. He grows his stretch by adding the next day on the right until the total reaches the target, then he trims days off the left as long as the total still meets the target, noting how short the stretch got. He keeps doing this across the whole history and remembers the shortest qualifying stretch.

**One line to remember:** Grow right until you hit the target, then shrink left as far as you can, tracking the smallest length.

sections.s2_technical:
Unlike the fixed-size window, here the window size changes dynamically based on a condition, which is the sum reaching the target. Because all numbers are positive, adding an element always increases the sum and removing one always decreases it, which is what makes the shrink step valid.

We keep a running sum starting at zero, a left pointer at the start, and a best length initialized to a value representing infinity. We expand the right pointer across the array, adding each element to the running sum. Whenever the running sum is greater than or equal to the target, we have a qualifying window, so we record its length if it is smaller than the best so far, then we shrink from the left by subtracting the left element and advancing the left pointer, continuing to shrink while the sum still meets the target. This inner shrink finds the shortest qualifying window ending at the current right position.

A finance usage example: suppose daily deposits are `[2, 1, 5, 2, 3, 2]` and the target is 7. Expanding, at some point the window `[2, 1, 5]` sums to 8, which meets 7, length 3; we shrink, dropping 2 to get `[1, 5]` summing to 6, which is below 7, so we stop shrinking with best length 2 recorded from `[5, 2]` later. Continuing, the window `[5, 2]` sums to 7 with length 2, and eventually `[3, 2]` or similar also meets 7 with length 2, so the smallest qualifying length is 2.

The senior-level nuance: if the best length was never updated, meaning no window ever reached the target, we return zero to signal that. The positivity of the numbers is essential; with negatives, growing the window would not monotonically increase the sum and the shrink logic would break, requiring a different approach such as prefix sums with a deque. Each pointer only moves forward, so although there is an inner shrink loop, the total work is linear because across the whole run the left pointer advances at most n times in total.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's treasury wants to raise at least a target amount of liquidity from a run of consecutive daily deposits, using the shortest possible stretch of days so the funds are gathered quickly. Scanning every possible stretch to find the shortest qualifying one is quadratic over long deposit histories.

Problem 2 — Because all daily deposits are positive, the treasury can use an efficient sliding window that grows and shrinks, avoiding the quadratic re-scan.

The code defines a `LiquidityWindowFinder` class with a `smallestWindowLength` method implementing the variable-size sliding window. A runnable demo seeds a deposit history and a target and logs the smallest qualifying window length.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the deposits `[2, 1, 5, 2, 3, 2]` and the target `7`.

Step 1: The finder sets the window sum to zero, the left pointer to index 0, and the best length to infinity.

Step 2: It expands the right pointer, adding 2, then 1, then 5, reaching a window sum of 8 across indices 0 to 2, which meets the target 7. The window length is 3, so best becomes 3. It shrinks by subtracting the left element 2, giving a window sum of 6, which is below 7, so shrinking stops with left at index 1.

Step 3: It expands to index 3, adding 2, so the window `[1, 5, 2]` sums to 8, meeting 7, length 3, which does not beat best 3. It shrinks by subtracting 1, giving `[5, 2]` summing to 7, still meeting the target, length 2, so best becomes 2. It shrinks again by subtracting 5, giving 2, below 7, so shrinking stops with left at index 3.

Step 4: It expands to index 4, adding 3, so `[2, 3]` sums to 5, below 7. It expands to index 5, adding 2, so `[2, 3, 2]` sums to 7, meeting the target, length 3, not beating best 2. It shrinks, dropping 2 to get `[3, 2]` summing to 5, below 7, so shrinking stops.

Step 5: The scan ends. The smallest qualifying window length recorded is 2, from the stretch `[5, 2]`, so the method returns 2.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:30:00 PM com.bank.treasury.LiquidityWindowDemo main
INFO: Deposits: [2, 1, 5, 2, 3, 2], target=7
INFO: Smallest window length meeting target 7 = 2
INFO: Shortest stretch to raise 7 spans 2 day(s).
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [2,1,5,2,3,2], target=7
    │ expand → [2,1,5] sum8 ≥7 len3 best=3; shrink → [1,5] sum6 <7
    │ expand → [1,5,2] sum8 ≥7; shrink → [5,2] sum7 len2 best=2; shrink → [2] <7
    │ expand → [2,3,2] sum7 len3 (no improve); shrink → [3,2] <7
    ▼
  smallest length = 2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The smallest-subarray-with-a-given-sum problem is the variable-size sliding window, and the key difference from the fixed-size version is that the window grows and shrinks dynamically based on a condition rather than staying a constant width. The condition here is the running sum reaching the target, and the technique works because all the numbers are positive, so adding an element always increases the sum and removing one always decreases it.

I keep a running sum, a left pointer at the start, and a best length initialized to infinity. I expand the right pointer across the array, adding each element to the running sum. The moment the sum reaches or exceeds the target, I have a qualifying window, so I record its length if it beats my best, and then I shrink from the left by subtracting the left element and advancing the left pointer, continuing to shrink as long as the sum still meets the target. That inner shrink finds the shortest qualifying window ending at the current right position, and sweeping the right pointer across the array finds the shortest overall.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the treasury team. We wanted to raise at least a target amount of liquidity from a run of consecutive daily deposits using the shortest possible stretch of days, so the funds could be gathered quickly. Over long deposit histories a quadratic scan of every stretch was too slow, and because the daily deposits were all positive, the grow-and-shrink sliding window gave the shortest qualifying stretch in a single linear pass.

The senior-level point I make is about the linear-time guarantee and the positivity assumption. Even though there is an inner shrink loop nested inside the outer expand loop, the total work is linear because across the entire run the left pointer only ever advances forward and can move at most as many times as there are elements. The positivity of the numbers is what makes the shrink step valid; with negative numbers the sum would not change monotonically and I would need a different technique such as prefix sums with a monotonic deque. I also return zero when no window ever reaches the target, which cleanly signals the no-solution case rather than returning a misleading length.
